title: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge wasn’t destroyed by simple resonance
body: In November 1940, just four months after opening, the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State twisted itself apart in a steady wind of about 64 km/h (40 mph). It is often called a textbook case of resonance, but engineers attribute the collapse mainly to aeroelastic flutter: the twisting deck changed how air flowed around it, which fed energy into ever larger twists. No person died; the only death was a dog left in a car.

slides.heading: Galloping Gertie
slides.text: From the time the deck was built, it rose and fell so much in wind that construction workers nicknamed it Galloping Gertie. Damping measures failed to stop it.

slides.heading: Why not resonance?
slides.text: Classic resonance needs pushes that arrive at a matching rhythm. A steady wind has no such rhythm. Here the motion itself shaped the forces: a self-feeding loop.

slides.heading: The lasting lesson
slides.text: Since then, major bridge designs are tested in wind tunnels, and decks are built stiffer or more aerodynamic, often with open trusses or streamlined box girders.

slides.question: Why don’t engineers call the collapse simple resonance?
options: A steady wind has no matching rhythm
The wind was far too weak that day
The deck was made of concrete
slides.explanation: Classic resonance needs pushes at a matching rhythm. Here the deck’s own twisting changed the airflow, which fed energy into ever larger twists: flutter.
